title: Extending Juniper Reach Library's Room-Booking Pilot
question: Synthetic development case: Using the fictional source brief below, write a short explanatory article or decision memo of approximately 300–350 words for library staff and residents. Explain the mixed pilot feedback, distinguish observations from alternative explanations, and make the reasoning, responsibilities and conditions for extending the pilot before considering expansion clear. Treat all numbers and decision thresholds as invented case facts or proposals. Keep synthetic-provenance labeling in the metadata and task question rather than in the intended article body.

synthetic_provenance.description: This independently invented development case describes a fictional institution, observations, feedback, responsibilities and proposed decision criteria. It is not a report of real events and uses no external sources.
synthetic_provenance.construction_constraints: The source brief and original were created for this case without reading writing skills, prior studies, detectors, other experiment files or holdouts. No candidate revision or detector scan was produced.
synthetic_provenance.original_authorship_context: The original is a complete explanatory draft for a fictional scenario; it claims no firsthand human experience.
synthetic_provenance.intended_use: One new development case for a writing-method comparison.

source_brief.audience: Library staff and residents considering how to evaluate the room-booking pilot.

facts.fact: Juniper Reach Library is a fictional community library running a room-booking pilot; the review concerns whether to extend that pilot before considering additional rooms.
The pilot has completed its first eight weeks.
The pilot offered two rooms, with free bookings lasting two hours, during staffed opening hours.
There were 160 available booking slots during the first eight weeks; 118 were reserved, 91 of those reservations were used, and 27 reserved slots were unused.
Forty-two people voluntarily submitted feedback; 25 valued having a predictable place for study or small-group work, and the other 17 reported difficulty finding a slot or completing a booking.
The feedback was voluntary rather than a representative survey, so it does not establish the prevalence of the reported concerns among all residents.
Eighteen of the 27 unused reservations were made by four repeat bookers.
Most of the slots that were never reserved fell before noon on weekdays.
The review notes treat the reservation count as evidence of demand, but the current observations do not establish reliable access for residents.
The review notes identify cancellation habits as a possible contributor to unused reservations; unused reservations do not by themselves establish the extent of unmet demand.
The review notes identify residents' availability at different times of day as a possible contributor to low weekday-morning demand; this explanation has not been tested.
Adding rooms would not necessarily resolve cancellation habits or a mismatch between residents' availability and the timing of unused slots.
The online booking form requires an email address; telephone bookings can currently be taken only when the front-desk supervisor is available.
Three of the 17 respondents who reported booking difficulties said that the email requirement or supervisor-only telephone coverage had prevented them from completing a booking.
The review proposal is to extend the pilot for six weeks before deciding whether to add rooms, using the extension to test improvements to access and booking reliability.
During the proposed extension, any trained desk worker would accept telephone and in-person reservations, and all booking routes would use the same room-slot inventory.
The proposal includes reminders and a simple cancellation option, intended to help residents release reservations they no longer need; their effectiveness has not been measured.

The service manager would arrange staff training and publish weekly totals for reservations, attendance, cancellations and requests that could not be accommodated, broken down by booking route and time of day.
Desk workers would record requests consistently, including requests received when the rooms were fully booked.
An expansion decision would follow the six-week extension, with expansion considered only if trained staff can cover every staffed opening period.
A further proposed condition for considering expansion is that at least 85% of reservations during the extension are either used or cancelled before their start time.
A further proposed condition for considering expansion is that requests that cannot be accommodated continue to be recorded in at least four of the six extension weeks despite the process changes.
Meeting all three proposed conditions would support considering expansion, but would not establish how many additional rooms are needed.
If staff coverage for access or booking reliability remains weak after the extension, the proposal is to revise the booking process and reassess before proceeding with expansion.

original:
Juniper Reach Library should extend its room-booking pilot for six weeks before deciding whether to add more rooms. The first eight weeks show demand, but they do not yet establish that residents can access the space reliably.

The pilot offered two rooms for free, two-hour bookings during staffed hours. Of 160 available slots, 118 were reserved and 91 were used. Among 42 feedback respondents, 25 valued a predictable place for study or small-group work, while 17 reported difficulties finding a slot or completing a booking. This voluntary feedback identifies concerns without establishing how common they are among all residents.

Two details complicate the reservation total. Eighteen of the 27 unused reservations came from four repeat bookers, and most unreserved slots fell before noon on weekdays. Missed bookings may reflect cancellation habits; low daytime use may reflect when residents can attend. More rooms would not necessarily address these possibilities.

Access needs a practical test. The online form requires an email address, and telephone bookings currently depend on the front-desk supervisor being available. Three respondents said these requirements prevented a booking. During an extension, any trained desk worker should accept telephone or in-person reservations using the same inventory as online bookings. Reminders and a simple cancellation option could help residents release slots they no longer need.

The service manager should arrange training and publish weekly reservation, attendance, cancellation and unfulfilled-request totals by booking route and time of day. Desk workers should record requests consistently, including those made when rooms are full.

An expansion decision should follow the six-week extension. The proposed conditions are that trained staff can cover every staffed opening period, at least 85% of reservations are used or cancelled before their start, and unfulfilled requests persist in at least four weeks despite the changes. These conditions would support considering expansion; they would not establish how many rooms are needed. If access coverage or booking reliability remains weak, the next step should be to revise the process and reassess.
